subject: Neurology
vignette: A neuroanatomy review is covering the contents of the cavernous sinus, which sits on either side of the pituitary and drains blood from the eye and superficial cortex into the internal jugular vein. The mnemonic 'I TOMATO' lists the structures that traverse it.
question: Which of the following structures does NOT pass through the cavernous sinus?
explanation_correct: The cavernous sinus contains the internal carotid artery and CNs III, IV, V1, V2, and VI, plus postganglionic sympathetic pupillary fibers en route to the orbit, remembered as 'I TOMATO.' CN II runs in the optic nerve above and anterior to the cavernous sinus and does not traverse it. Blood from the eye and superficial cortex drains through the sinus to the internal jugular vein.

explanation_incorrect.A: The internal carotid artery passes through the cavernous sinus as the 'I' of I TOMATO and is the site of carotid-cavernous fistulas.
explanation_incorrect.C: CN VI travels through the cavernous sinus and is commonly affected in cavernous sinus syndrome, producing impaired abduction.
explanation_incorrect.D: CN IV is one of the nerves within the cavernous sinus and its involvement contributes to ophthalmoplegia.
explanation_incorrect.E: The ophthalmic division of CN V passes through the cavernous sinus and carries corneal sensation, which is reduced in cavernous sinus syndrome.

educationalObjective: The cavernous sinus contains the ICA and CN III, IV, V1, V2, and VI (I TOMATO), but not CN II.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 45-year-old man with a pituitary macroadenoma has right-sided ophthalmoplegia, decreased sensation over the right cornea, and right ptosis with miosis. Imaging shows tumor extension into the cavernous sinus. The clinician diagnoses cavernous sinus syndrome.
question: Which structure's involvement best explains the loss of corneal sensation in this patient?
explanation_correct: The ophthalmic division of CN V supplies sensory innervation to the cornea and travels through the cavernous sinus. Its involvement in cavernous sinus syndrome reduces corneal sensation. The accompanying ophthalmoplegia reflects CN III, IV, and VI involvement, and the ptosis with miosis reflects interruption of postganglionic sympathetic fibers; pituitary mass effect is a classic cause.

explanation_incorrect.A: CN III is motor to most extraocular muscles and carries parasympathetic fibers; it does not supply corneal sensation.
explanation_incorrect.B: CN IV supplies only the superior oblique muscle and carries no sensory fibers from the cornea.
explanation_incorrect.C: CN VI innervates the lateral rectus; its involvement causes impaired abduction but not loss of corneal sensation.
explanation_incorrect.E: CN II is the sensory nerve for vision and does not traverse the cavernous sinus or carry corneal sensation.

educationalObjective: Reduced corneal sensation in cavernous sinus syndrome reflects involvement of the ophthalmic division of CN V.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A patient develops cavernous sinus thrombosis after a facial infection spreads retrograde into the cranial vena cava. The infectious emboli travel freely through the dural venous sinuses. A medical student asks which property of these sinuses accounts for the ease of spread.
question: Which of the following features of dural venous sinuses facilitates this spread of infection?

options.text: The absence of valves within them
Their direct connection to the cerebral aqueduct
Their location within the brain parenchyma

explanation_correct: Dural venous sinuses lack valves, so blood and infected material can flow in either direction. This allows infection from the face or paranasal sinuses to spread retrograde into the cavernous sinus, producing thrombosis. The resulting cavernous sinus syndrome can include ophthalmoplegia, decreased corneal sensation, and Horner syndrome.

explanation_incorrect.A: Valves would limit retrograde flow and actually protect against the spread of infection, which is why their absence matters here.
explanation_incorrect.B: Dural venous sinuses are low-pressure venous channels, not high-pressure arterial structures.
explanation_incorrect.D: The cerebral aqueduct connects the third and fourth ventricles and is not part of the venous sinus system.
explanation_incorrect.E: Dural venous sinuses lie between layers of dura, not within the brain parenchyma.

educationalObjective: Dural venous sinuses lack valves, permitting retrograde spread of infection that can cause cavernous sinus thrombosis.
